lines.raw: RCM metrics.
lines.say: R C M metrics.

lines.raw: RCM metrics measure **how fast** a provider turns care into cash, **how cleanly** its claims go through, and **how much** of the money it is owed it actually collects.
lines.say: R C M metrics measure how fast a provider turns care into cash, how cleanly its claims go through, and how much of the money it is owed it actually collects.

lines.raw: Hospital finance teams report them to leadership, and lenders look at them too.

lines.raw: Industry groups such as the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) publish standard definitions so providers can compare themselves fairly.

lines.raw: Which metric answers which question.
lines.say: Which metric answers which question.

lines.raw: **Days in AR**. Question it answers: How many days of charges are waiting to be collected? If it gets worse, look first at: Follow-up, denials, slow payers.
lines.say: Days in A R. Question it answers: How many days of charges are waiting to be collected? If it gets worse, look first at: Follow-up, denials, slow payers.

lines.raw: **Clean claim rate**. Question it answers: What share of claims go out with no errors the first time? If it gets worse, look first at: Front end and mid cycle data quality.
lines.say: Clean claim rate. Question it answers: What share of claims go out with no errors the first time? If it gets worse, look first at: Front end and mid cycle data quality.

lines.raw: **Initial denial rate**. Question it answers: What share of claims does the insurer deny the first time? If it gets worse, look first at: Denial root causes (lesson 5).
lines.say: Initial denial rate. Question it answers: What share of claims does the insurer deny the first time? If it gets worse, look first at: Denial root causes (lesson 5).

lines.raw: **Net collection rate**. Question it answers: Of the money we are owed after contract discounts, how much do we collect? If it gets worse, look first at: Denial write-offs, unpaid patient balances.
lines.say: Net collection rate. Question it answers: Of the money we are owed after contract discounts, how much do we collect? If it gets worse, look first at: Denial write-offs, unpaid patient balances.

lines.raw: **AR over 90 days**. Question it answers: How much of AR is old and at risk? If it gets worse, look first at: Follow-up on stuck claims.
lines.say: A R over 90 days. Question it answers: How much of A R is old and at risk? If it gets worse, look first at: Follow-up on stuck claims.

lines.raw: **Point-of-service collection rate**. Question it answers: How much of the patient share due at the visit is collected there? If it gets worse, look first at: Front desk processes.
lines.say: Point-of-service collection rate. Question it answers: How much of the patient share due at the visit is collected there? If it gets worse, look first at: Front desk processes.

lines.raw: Days in AR.
lines.say: Days in A R.

lines.raw: Days in AR equals Total AR ÷ Average daily charges   (average daily charges equals charges over the last 90 days ÷ 90).
lines.say: Days in A R equals Total A R ÷ Average daily charges (average daily charges equals charges over the last 90 days ÷ 90).

lines.raw: For example: Sunrise Family Clinic, 31 March 2025: AR $100,000.
lines.say: For example: Sunrise Family Clinic, 31 March 2025: A R 100000 dollars.

lines.raw: Charges January to March $300,000 ÷ 90 equals $3,333 a day.
lines.say: Charges January to March 300000 dollars ÷ 90 equals 3333 dollars a day.

lines.raw: Days in AR equals $100,000 ÷ $3,333 equals 30 days.
lines.say: Days in A R equals 100000 dollars ÷ 3333 dollars equals 30 days.

lines.raw: Clean claim rate.
lines.say: Clean claim rate.

lines.raw: Clean claim rate equals Claims accepted first time with no edits or rejections ÷ All claims sent.
lines.say: Clean claim rate equals Claims accepted first time with no edits or rejections ÷ All claims sent.

lines.raw: For example: April 2025: 1,880 of 2,000 claims passed with no changes equals 94%.
lines.say: For example: April 2025: 1,880 of 2,000 claims passed with no changes equals 94 percent.

lines.raw: Initial denial rate.
lines.say: Initial denial rate.

lines.raw: Initial denial rate equals Claims denied on first processing ÷ Claims processed.
lines.say: Initial denial rate equals Claims denied on first processing ÷ Claims processed.

lines.raw: For example: April 2025: 160 denied ÷ 2,000 equals 8%.
lines.say: For example: April 2025: 160 denied ÷ 2,000 equals 8 percent.

lines.raw: Net collection rate.
lines.say: Net collection rate.

lines.raw: Net collection rate equals Payments ÷ (Charges − Contractual adjustments).
lines.say: Net collection rate equals Payments ÷ (Charges − Contractual adjustments).

lines.raw: For example: Payments $190,000 ÷ ($300,000 charges − $100,000 contract discounts) equals $190,000 ÷ $200,000 equals 95%.
lines.say: For example: Payments 190000 dollars ÷ (300000 dollars charges − 100000 dollars contract discounts) equals 190000 dollars ÷ 200000 dollars equals 95 percent.

lines.raw: The other 5% was lost to denial write-offs and unpaid patient balances.
lines.say: The other 5 percent was lost to denial write-offs and unpaid patient balances.

lines.raw: AR over 90 days.
lines.say: A R over 90 days.

lines.raw: AR over 90 days % equals AR older than 90 days ÷ Total AR.
lines.say: A R over 90 days % equals A R older than 90 days ÷ Total A R.

lines.raw: For example: From the aging report in lesson 4: ($6,000 plus $5,000) ÷ $100,000 equals 11%.
lines.say: For example: From the aging report in lesson 4: (6000 dollars plus 5000 dollars) ÷ 100000 dollars equals 11 percent.

lines.raw: Why gross collection rate misleads.
lines.say: Why gross collection rate misleads.

lines.raw: **Gross collection rate** = payments ÷ charges.
lines.say: Gross collection rate = payments ÷ charges.
Here 190000 dollars ÷ 300000 dollars = 63 percent.

lines.raw: That looks terrible, but most of the gap is the **contract discount** the clinic agreed to and never expected to collect.
lines.say: That looks terrible, but most of the gap is the contract discount the clinic agreed to and never expected to collect.

lines.raw: Because charges are list prices, gross collection rate mostly measures how high the chargemaster is, not how well the clinic collects.
lines.say: Because charges are list prices, gross collection rate mostly measures how high the chargemaster is, not how well the clinic collects.

lines.raw: Use **net** collection rate to judge performance.
lines.say: Use net collection rate to judge performance.

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: **Different definitions**. What goes wrong: "Clean claim" may mean passing the scrubber, or accepted by the insurer, or paid with no rework. What to do: Write the definition down and use it every month.
lines.say: Different definitions. What goes wrong: "Clean claim" may mean passing the scrubber, or accepted by the insurer, or paid with no rework. What to do: Write the definition down and use it every month.

lines.raw: **Resubmissions counted as new claims**. What goes wrong: A rejected claim sent twice counts as two claims and inflates the denominator. What to do: Count original claims; track versions separately.
lines.say: Resubmissions counted as new claims. What goes wrong: A rejected claim sent twice counts as two claims and inflates the denominator. What to do: Count original claims; track versions separately.

lines.raw: **Line vs claim vs dollars**. What goes wrong: One denied line on a 5-line claim: is the claim denied? What to do: Report denial rates by claim and by dollars, and say which.
lines.say: Line versus claim versus dollars. What goes wrong: One denied line on a 5-line claim: is the claim denied? What to do: Report denial rates by claim and by dollars, and say which.

lines.raw: **Timing mismatch**. What goes wrong: Payments this month are for charges from earlier months. What to do: Use rolling periods, or match payments back to their service month.
lines.say: Timing mismatch. What goes wrong: Payments this month are for charges from earlier months. What to do: Use rolling periods, or match payments back to their service month.

lines.raw: **Credit balances in AR**. What goes wrong: Overpayments are negative AR and make AR look smaller. What to do: Report credit balances separately.
lines.say: Credit balances in A R. What goes wrong: Overpayments are negative A R and make A R look smaller. What to do: Report credit balances separately.

lines.raw: **Charge changes**. What goes wrong: A price increase raises charges and lowers days in AR without any real change. What to do: Watch for chargemaster updates when trends jump.
lines.say: Charge changes. What goes wrong: A price increase raises charges and lowers days in A R without any real change. What to do: Watch for chargemaster updates when trends jump.
